##Part B — Subsetting (Accessing) Vectors
```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")


# Access the 3rd element using positional indexing

grades[3]


# Access the 1st and 4th elements using positional indexing

grades[c(1, 4)]


# Access "Science" and "PE" together using their names

grades[c("Science", "PE")]
```

#Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.
Logical Indexing Scenario: Logical indexing is ideal when you want to filter data based on a dynamic condition or threshold where you don't know the exact indices beforehand (e.g., filtering out student records where scores fall below a passing grade of 75, or selecting transactions over $1,000).

Question #7:
Print a vector with the integers between 1 and 100 that are not divisible by 3, 5 and 7 using filter option.
```{r}
Filter(function(i) { all(i %% c(3, 5, 7) != 0) }, seq(100))
```

Question 3
```{r}
fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")

# Add "date" to the end of fruits
append(fruits, "date")
# Output: [1] "apple"  "banana" "cherry" "date"  

# Insert "kiwi" after position 1 (between "apple" and "banana")
append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)
# Output: [1] "apple"  "kiwi"   "banana" "cherry"
```
# Question #8:
# - In the vectors-recycling chunk, z has 6 elements and short has only 2. R still produced an answer instead of an error.
R’s recycling rule automatically repeated the elements of the shorter vector ("short") 
from the beginning until it matched the length of the longer vector ("z").  Since z had 6 elements and short had 2 (1, 0), R recycled short three times 
to make it (1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0) so it could perform element-wise addition.

#Question 9: Now try adding z (length 6) to c(1, 0, 1) (length 3) instead. Does it work cleanly?
Yes, it works cleanly and without any warnings. Because the length of the longer vector (6) 
is an exact multiple of the shorter vector (3), R recycles c(1, 0, 1) twice smoothly 
(resulting in 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1) to match z's length. R only throws a warning message when 
the longer vector's length is not a multiple of the shorter vector's length.

# --- 1. Create the student list ---
```{r}
student <- list(
  name = "Maria Santos",
  age = 20,
  grades = c(88, 92, 79),
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)

# --- 2. Access "grades" using single brackets and check its type ---
student["grades"]
class(student["grades"])
# Output type: "list" (Single brackets return a sub-list)

# --- 3. Access "grades" using double brackets and check its type ---
student[["grades"]]
class(student[["grades"]])
# Output type: "numeric" (Double brackets unwrap/extract the underlying vector)


# --- 4. Access "name" using the $ operator ---
student$name
# Output: [1] "Maria Santos"


# --- 5. Extract the second grade in a single expression ---
student[["grades"]][2]
# Alternatively: student$grades[2]
# Output: [1] 92
```
#Question 10
student["grades"] uses single brackets ([) to return a sublist. The outer list structure is preserved, so running class() will return "list".

student[["grades"]] uses double brackets ([[) to extract the actual contents inside that list element. The outer list container is dropped, so running class() will return the class of the underlying object itself (such as "numeric", "character", or "data.frame").

#Question 11
Vectors only hold one data type so [ is enough, but lists can contain mixed or nested structures (like data frames or other lists), so R needs [ to keep the container and [[ to actually reach inside and grab what's stored there.

##Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
```

# TODO: Using what you learned in Parts B and D, print only the items
# (from inventory$item) that are currently in stock (in_stock == TRUE)
```{r}
print(inventory[["item"]][inventory[["in_stock"]] == TRUE])
```

# TODO: A new product "Ruler" priced at 15.00 and in stock (TRUE) needs
# to be added to inventory. Use append() to add "Ruler" to
# inventory$item, 15.00 to inventory$price, and TRUE to inventory$in_stock.
```{r}
inventory[["item"]] <- append(inventory[["item"]], "Ruler")
inventory[["price"]] <- append(inventory[["price"]], 15.00)
inventory[["in_stock"]] <- append(inventory[["in_stock"]], TRUE)
```


#Question 12
Even though item and in_stock are separate elements in the list, R evaluates inventory[["in_stock"]] first to create a logical filter, lines the elements up by their matching positions, and applies that filter mask to inventory[["item"]] to extract only the elements where the value is TRUE.


#Question 13
Storing related data as separate vectors is risky because if you accidentally sort, reorder, or update one vector without the others, the data gets completely misaligned and mismatched, whereas using a list keeps everything bundled together so they stay synchronized. Additionally, if you accidentally add or delete items from one vector and forget another, length mismatches will cause silent errors or weird recycling bugs in your code.


#Conclusion
Vectors can only store one type of data like all numbers or all text, while lists are much more flexible because they can hold mixed data types and even complex objects like data frames or other lists. Because lists have that extra outer container, you use double brackets [[ ]] to get the actual data inside and single brackets [ ] if you just want a smaller list, whereas vectors only need [ ]. I would use a vector when working with a plain, uniform set of data like a list of ages or test scores, but I'd choose a list whenever I need to package different types of related information together into one organized structure.
